text:
As presently conceived, the objectives of RISP will be pursued during a three-year field operation on the Ross Ice Shelf. The main effort will involve drilling through the Ross Ice Shelf to allow access to the water column and the sea floor below. A tentative drill site was selected at 82°30'S, 166°W (Fig. 1), based on the present knowledge of ice thickness (500-m), sub-shelf water depth (200-m), position on a West Antarctic ice flowline, and distance from the front of the ice shelf (400-km).
The first year's efforts commenced during the 1973-74 austral summer. Geophysical and glaciological techniques were employed to define the details of that portion of the Ross Ice Shelf where possible drill sites have been suggested. A grid network of stations, roughly 50-km apart, were occupied and located accurately through the use of a satellite navigation system. A small base camp for 16 people was established at the tentative drill site and overnight subsidiary camps were used on several occasions. LC-130 aircraft were used to deploy and supply the party from McMurdo Station. The main mode of transport in the field was a DeHavilland Twin Otter supplemented by oversnow vehicles for local work.
Information gathered during this first season of RISP will require a slight repositioning of the drill site. A drill camp will be established at 82°22'S, 168°40'W and the old base camp will be dismantled and removed.
During the 1974-75 austral summer the geophysical and glaciological survey was continued. Temporary base camps were established for portions of the season close to 80°07'S, 160°41'W, and at about 80°30'S, 175°30'E. LC-130 aircraft, Twin Otter, and motor toboggans are utilized for transportation.
